h1: The 5 Best Reclining Office Chairs with Footrests of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Reclining Office Chairs: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: five reclining office chairs with built-in footrests, covering weight limits, lumbar support, headrests and seat comfort.
summary: The GTPLAYER Big and Tall is the best reclining office chair with a footrest: 400 lb rating, a footrest that locks extended and a near-flat recline. The N-GEN is the budget pick with adjustable lumbar. The headrest GTPLAYER suits long reading sessions, while the Homall adds a massage cushion that matters less than its structure. The fleece chair is for cross-legged sitters.
intro: Most chairs advertised with a footrest are gaming-style recliners, and that is where this category quietly goes wrong. The footrest is usually a thin steel tray bolted to the seat frame, and when a heavier person leans back, the whole load shifts rearward through a mechanism never designed for it. Rated capacity, not styling, decides whether a recliner survives a year.

We reviewed five chairs that genuinely ship with a footrest, dropping mesh and executive models that only mention one in passing. Each was scored on the Primea framework from listing specs: footrest locking, recline range, lumbar design, headrest and stated weight rating. Where a listing omits a rating, we marked the chair down for that gap, since an unrated recliner is a gamble.

products.name: GTPLAYER Big and Tall Gaming Chair 400lbs Heavy Duty Office Chair with Foot Rest & Ergonomic Pocket Spring Lumbar Support
products.verdict: High weight rating, a locking footrest and near-flat recline.
products.description:
The GTPLAYER Big and Tall is the only chair here that publishes a 400 lb weight rating, and that number matters more than any comfort feature. The rating reflects the gas lift, base and frame, so it shows how much margin sits behind the recline mechanism. The footrest pulls out and locks extended, and the pocket spring lumbar cushion gives with your spine.

It ranks first because it fixes the two classic failures of gaming recliners: a wobbling leg rest and an unrated frame. The N-GEN costs less but lists no rating. The headrest GTPLAYER also costs less, yet its lumbar is a plain cushion.

Buy it if you are a larger user who wants a near-flat recline. The caveat is floor space: fully reclined, it needs real clearance, and it is the priciest of the gaming trio.
cons: Highest price of the gaming trio
products.idealFor: Larger users who want full recline.

products.name: N-GEN GAMING Video Gaming Chair with Footrest Lumbar Support for Home Office High Back Recliner
products.verdict: A real footrest and height-adjustable lumbar for less.
products.description:
The N-GEN is the one budget chair here with height-adjustable lumbar, and that feature separates it from the pack. A fixed cushion fits only one spine shape. Sliding the support up or down lets you land it at the small of your back, where most office-chair fatigue starts. A pull-out footrest and 360 degree swivel base round out the sheet.

It takes second over the headrest GTPLAYER because adjustable lumbar beats a headrest for people who sit upright most of the day. It trails the Big and Tall because its listing gives no weight rating, a real gap on a recliner.

Buy it if you are an average-size adult spending under $100. The caveat: leather-look upholstery can peel over time, so keep it out of direct sun.
products.skipIf: You need a stated heavy-duty rating.

products.name: GTPLAYER Gaming Chair, Computer Chair with Footrest and Lumbar Support, Height Adjustable with 360-Swivel Seat and Headrest
products.verdict: Adds an adjustable headrest to the footrest and recline.
products.description:
This GTPLAYER earns its spot through the neck, not the back. The adjustable headrest, pull-out footrest and reclining backrest combine into a lounge setup, while the gas lift and 360 degree swivel keep it usable at a desk. Once a chair reclines, a headrest stops being decoration: without one, your neck does the work.

It lands third because its lumbar is a standard cushion, so it cannot match the N-GEN's adjustable support or the Big and Tall's pocket spring. It beats the Homall by skipping the vibration gimmick and leaving less to break, though both share the $50 to $100 bucket.

Buy it for long stretches of reading or viewing with the chair leaned back. The caveat is the missing weight rating, which makes it a poor bet for heavier users.

products.name: Homall Gaming Chair, Video Game Chair with Footrest and Massage Lumbar Support, Height Adjustable with Swivel Seat and Headrest
products.verdict: A vibrating lumbar cushion on top of recline and footrest.
products.description:
The Homall stacks a vibrating massage lumbar cushion on the basics: pull-out footrest, adjustable headrest and reclining backrest. Vibration motors in a seat cushion produce a light buzz, not kneading, so treat it as a pleasant extra rather than back therapy. The height-adjustable swivel base keeps it workable at a desk.

It ranks fourth because the extra feature has no structural counterpart. The listing offers no weight rating or frame detail, leaving it indistinguishable from the headrest GTPLAYER one spot up, and that chair skips the electronics. If the massage module fails, you hold a plain recliner.

Buy it if you enjoy light lumbar vibration and use the chair casually. Skip it if proven back support is the goal, because a pocket spring or adjustable cushion does more for posture than a buzzing pad.

products.name: Big and Tall Office Chair, Flip Armrests for Pets & Cross Legged Sitting, Executive Ergonomic Chair with Foot Rest, Teddy Fleece Wide Seat
products.verdict: Wide soft seat with flip-up armrests for different postures.
products.description:
This is the odd chair in the ranking, on purpose. A wide teddy fleece seat and flip-up armrests are designed around how people actually sit: cross-legged, side-saddle or sharing the cushion with a pet. Flip-up arms remove the barrier that makes those postures awkward. The executive high back, reclining backrest and included footrest finish the package.

It finishes last for two reasons. It sits in the $200 to $500 bucket, well above every GTPLAYER, and the listing gives no weight rating or lumbar detail to justify the premium. The Big and Tall offers 400 lbs of stated capacity and pocket spring lumbar for less.

Buy it if posture freedom matters more than structure. The caveat is the fleece itself: it traps hair and dust, and runs warm in summer.

whatMatters.detail: The footrest is the feature that defines this category, and locking is what separates a usable one from a wobbly tray. A pull-out rest that locks extended holds firm when you press your heels down, while an unlocked one drifts. Read the spec bullets for the words locks or locking, and be cautious when the listing only says footrest included.

Weight capacity is the rating of the gas lift, base and frame working together, not just the seat. A recliner shifts load backward and concentrates it on the tilt mechanism, so a chair rated at 400 lbs carries real margin for an average adult. Look for a stated number in pounds, and treat a missing rating as a warning sign.

Recline range is how far the backrest tilts, from a slight lean to a near-flat bed position. Deeper recline suits napping but needs clearance behind the chair, which matters in a small office. Check for the phrase near-flat or an angle in degrees in the specs, and measure the space behind your desk before you buy.

Lumbar support is the contour that fills the curve of your lower back. A plain cushion stays where it is, adjustable support moves up and down to match your spine, and pocket spring designs add give under pressure. These differ more than the label suggests, so scan the specs for adjustable, height-adjustable or pocket spring wording.

A headrest matters once you lean back, because your neck loses the support the upright backrest gave it. An adjustable headrest lets you position it behind your skull rather than your shoulders, which cuts strain on long reclined sessions. Confirm that the listing says adjustable rather than just headrest, and that the chair actually includes the pillow.

faq.q: Can these chairs be used as office chairs?
faq.a: Yes. The N-GEN, Homall and both GTPLAYER models all swivel and adjust in height, so they work at a desk. Their look is gaming-style rather than corporate, so check that the arms clear your desktop before relying on one for daily work.

Assuming every chair in a gaming listing includes a footrest. Mesh and executive models often leave it out or sell it separately. Confirm that the Homall, N-GEN or GTPLAYER you choose lists a pull-out footrest, and check for locking.

faq.q: Is the 400 lb model worth it?
faq.a: Only if you need the rating or a near-flat recline. The GTPLAYER Big and Tall carries a 400 lb rating and costs more than the other gaming chairs. Average-size users can save money with the N-GEN or the headrest GTPLAYER.

faq.q: How do I set the recline?
faq.a: Use the lever beneath the seat to release the backrest, lean to the angle you want, and let go to lock it. Extend the footrest on the GTPLAYER or Homall before leaning back so your legs share the load.

faq.q: How do I maintain the footrest?
faq.a: Check the locking mechanism and footrest hinge periodically, and never stand on the footrest. On the Homall, keep the massage cushion's wiring dry. For the leather-look N-GEN, wipe with a damp cloth and avoid direct sunlight.

Not easily. Fleece traps hair and dust, so vacuum the seat regularly and spot-clean with a damp cloth. If you share the chair with a pet, expect more frequent upkeep than the leather-look N-GEN or the GTPLAYER chairs.

finalTake: For most buyers, the GTPLAYER Big and Tall is the chair to pick: a 400 lb rating, a locking footrest and near-flat recline cover the failures common in this category. Average builds on a budget should look at the N-GEN for its adjustable lumbar. Choose the headrest GTPLAYER for long reclined sessions and the fleece chair only for cross-legged sitting. Verify the weight rating before ordering.
